38|BACKGROUND
39|Abiraterone acetate, a drug that blocks endogenous androgen synthesis, plus predni-
40|sone is indicated for metastatic castration-resistant prostate cancer. We evaluated the
41|clinical benefit of abiraterone acetate plus prednisone with androgen-deprivation ther
42|apy in patients with newly diagnosed, metastatic, castration-sensitive prostate cancer.
43|METHODS
44|In this double-blind, placebo-controlled, phase 3 trial, we randomly assigned 1199 pa-
45|tients to receive either androgen-deprivation therapy plus abiraterone acetate (1000 mg
46|daily, given once daily as four 250-mg tablets) plus prednisone (5 mg daily) (the
47|abiraterone group) or androgen-deprivation therapy plus dual placebos (the placebo
48|group). The two primary end points were overall survival and radiographic progression-
49|free survival.
50|RESULTS
51|After a median follow-up of 30.4 months at a planned interim analysis (after 406 pa-
52|tients had died), the median overall survival was significantly longer in the abiraterone
53|group than in the placebo group (not reached vs. 34.7 months) (hazard ratio for death,
54|0.62; 95% confidence interval [CI], 0.51 to 0.76; P<0.001). The median length of radio-
55|graphic progression-free survival was 33.0 months in the abiraterone group and 14.8
56|months in the placebo group (hazard ratio for disease progression or death, 0.47; 95%
57|CI, 0.39 to 0.55; P<0.001). Significantly better outcomes in all secondary end points
58|were observed in the abiraterone group, including the time until pain progression, next
59|subsequent therapy for prostate cancer, initiation of chemotherapy, and prostate-
60|specific antigen progression (P<0.001 for all comparisons), along with next symptom-
61|atic skeletal events (P = 0.009). These findings led to the unanimous recommendation
62|by the independent data and safety monitoring committee that the trial be unblinded
63|and crossover be allowed for patients in the placebo group to receive abiraterone. Rates
64|of grade 3 hypertension and hypokalemia were higher in the abiraterone group.
65|CONCLUSIONS
66|The addition of abiraterone acetate and prednisone to androgen-deprivation therapy
67|significantly increased overall survival and radiographic progression-free survival in
68|men with newly diagnosed, metastatic, castration-sensitive prostate cancer. (Funded
69|by Janssen Research and Development; LATITUDE ClinicalTrials.gov number,
70|NCT01715285.)

3|Abiraterone plus Prednisone in Prostate Cancer
4|M
5|etastatic, castration-sensitive
6|prostate cancer accounts for approxi-
7|mately 3% of all new prostate-cancer
8|diagnoses in the United States.1 Historically,
9|androgen-deprivation therapy consisting of bilat-
10|eral orchiectomy or luteinizing hormone-releas-
11|ing hormone analogues, with or without first-
12|generation androgen-receptor inhibitors, has been
13|the standard of care.2 Although the majority of
14|patients have an initial response to androgen-
15|deprivation therapy, most men with metastases
16|have progression to castration-resistant prostate
17|cancer within a median of approximately 1 year.3-5
18|Resistance to androgen-deprivation therapy is
19|largely driven by the reactivation of androgen-
20|receptor signaling through persistent adrenal an-
21|drogen production, up-regulation of intratumoral
22|testosterone production, modification of the bi-
23|ologic characteristics of androgen receptors, and
24|steroidogenic parallel pathways.2
25|The clinical benefit of adding docetaxel to
26|androgen-deprivation therapy versus treatment
27|with androgen-deprivation therapy alone has been
28|shown in three randomized, phase 3 trials -
29|Chemohormonal Therapy Versus Androgen Ab-
30|lation Randomized Trial for Extensive Disease in
31|Prostate Cancer (CHAARTED),5,6 Systemic Ther-
32|apy in Advancing or Metastatic Prostate Cancer:
33|Evaluation of Drug Efficacy (STAMPEDE),7 and
34|GETUG-153,8 - which collectively included more
35|than 3000 men with metastatic, castration-sensi-
36|tive prostate cancer. Androgen-deprivation ther-
37|apy plus docetaxel is now a standard of care for
38|men with metastatic, castration-sensitive pros-
39|tate cancer who are eligible for chemotherapy,
40|particularly those with a high metastatic burden,
41|as defined in the respective studies.9-11 Barriers
42|to the use of docetaxel include advanced patient
43|age, poor performance status, coexisting illness-
44|es, and patient preferences.9,12 Retrospective analy-
45|ses exploring real-world practice patterns13,14 indi-
46|cate that men with newly diagnosed, metastatic,
47|castration-sensitive prostate cancer who are not
48|being treated in clinical trials may be nearly a
49|decade older than those treated in clinical trials.
50|The concern with respect to chemotherapy-related
51|toxicity and the effect of coexisting illnesses on
52|complications is based on the severity of the
53|toxicity that has been observed. Chemotherapy-
54|related deaths were documented in all three
55|randomized trials in which docetaxel was added
56|to androgen-deprivation therapy.3,5,7
57|Abiraterone acetate, the prodrug of abiraterone,
58|inhibits cytochrome P-450c17, a critical enzyme
59|in androgen biosynthesis.15,16 Recent studies im-
60|plicate its active D4A metabolite in antitumor
61|effects, presumably through blockade of multi-
62|ple steroidogenic enzymes and antagonism of the
63|androgen receptor.17 Abiraterone acetate (here-
64|after referred to as abiraterone) in combination
65|with prednisone has been shown to significantly
66|increase overall survival and provide additional
67|clinical benefits in patients with metastatic,
68|castration-resistant prostate cancer who have
69|not received chemotherapy and in those who
70|have received previous docetaxel.18-22 The combi-
71|nation of abiraterone plus prednisone and andro-
72|gen-deprivation therapy has been shown to reduce
73|tumor burden in men with high-risk, localized
74|prostate cancer who are receiving neoadjuvant
75|therapy, which suggests a potential role for
76|inhibiting extragonadal androgen biosynthesis
77|before the emergence of castration resistance in
78|men with newly diagnosed, metastatic, castration-
79|sensitive prostate cancer.23,24 In LATITUDE, a
80|multinational, randomized, double-blind, placebo-
81|controlled, phase 3 trial, we evaluated the addition
82|of abiraterone plus prednisone to androgen-
83|deprivation therapy, as compared with androgen-
84|deprivation therapy and dual placebos, on overall
85|survival, radiographic progression-free survival,
86|and clinically relevant measures in men with
87|newly diagnosed, metastatic, castration-sensitive
88|prostate cancer.
89|Methods
90|Trial Design and Conduct
91|The trial was conducted at 235 sites in 34 coun-
92|tries in Europe, the Asia-Pacific region, Latin
93|America, and Canada. The trial protocol (avail-
94|able with the full text of this article at NEJM.org)
95|was approved by the review board at each par-
96|ticipating institution. The trial was conducted
97|according to the principles of the Declaration of
98|Helsinki and the International Conference on
99|Harmonisation Good Clinical Practice Guide-
100|lines. All the patients provided written informed
101|consent.
102|An independent data and safety monitoring
103|committee was commissioned by the sponsor,
104|Janssen Research and Development, to review
105|safety data on a regular basis and review effi-
106|cacy data at planned interim analyses. The trial

13|authors had full access to all parts of the data
14|and drafted the manuscript with sponsor input,
15|and all the coauthors subsequently provided in-
16|put. The sponsor provided funding for editorial
17|assistance. All the authors and participating in-
18|stitutions have agreements with the sponsor re-
19|garding data confidentiality.
20|Patients and Treatments
21|Eligible patients were required to be at least 18
22|years of age and to have an Eastern Cooperative
23|Oncology Group (ECOG) performance-status
24|score of 0 to 2 (on a 5-point scale, with higher
25|numbers indicating greater disability) with new-
26|ly diagnosed (≤3 months before randomization),
27|pathologically confirmed prostate cancer with-
28|out neuroendocrine differentiation or small-cell
29|histologic features. All the patients had high-risk,
30|metastatic, castration-sensitive prostate cancer,
31|as documented by a positive bone scan or meta-
32|static lesions at the time of diagnosis on com-
33|puted tomography (CT) or magnetic resonance
34|imaging (MRI), according to Response Evaluation
35|Criteria in Solid Tumors (RECIST), version 1.1.
36|In addition, the patients were required to have at
37|least two of the three following high-risk factors
38|associated with poor prognosis: a Gleason score
39|of 8 or more (on a scale of 2 to 10, with higher
40|scores indicating more aggressive disease), at
41|least three bone lesions, and the presence of
42|measurable visceral metastasis. Patients were
43|excluded if they had received previous chemo-
44|therapy, radiation therapy, or surgery for meta-
45|static prostate cancer, with the exception of
46|3 months or less of androgen-deprivation ther
47|apy with luteinizing hormone-releasing hormone
48|analogues or orchiectomy with or without con-
49|current first-generation androgen-receptor antag-
50|onists before baseline or one course of palliative
51|radiation or surgical therapy to treat symptoms
52|associated with metastatic disease.
53|Patients were randomly assigned in a 1:1 ratio
54|to receive androgen-deprivation therapy and abira
55|terone acetate (1000 mg daily, given once daily
56|as four 250-mg tablets) and prednisone (5 mg
57|daily) (the abiraterone group) or androgen-depri-
58|vation therapy and placebos (the placebo group).
59|Patients were stratified according to the presence
60|or absence of measurable visceral disease and
61|ECOG performance-status score (0 or 1 vs. 2).
62|Abiraterone or placebo was administered at least
63|1 hour before or 2 hours after a meal. All the
64|patients who had not undergone surgical castra-
65|tion received ongoing androgen-deprivation ther-
66|apy to reach or maintain a serum testosterone
67|level of less than 50 ng per deciliter (1.7 nmol
68|per liter). Safety and dosing adherence were
69|evaluated during each trial visit, at treatment
70|discontinuation (if applicable), and at the end-of-
71|trial visit.
72|End Points
73|The two primary efficacy end points were overall
74|survival and radiographic progression-free sur-
75|vival. Overall survival was defined as the time
76|from randomization to death from any cause,
77|and radiographic progression-free survival as the
78|time from randomization to the occurrence of
79|radiographic progression or death from any
80|cause. Radiographic progression of soft-tissue
81|lesions was evaluated by either CT or MRI on the
82|basis of RECIST, version 1.1. Progression on
83|bone scanning was assessed by adaptation of
84|Prostate Cancer Working Group 2 criteria (Table
85|S1 in the Supplementary Appendix, available at
86|NEJM.org).25 Potential bias favoring the abirater
87|one group in the assessment of radiographic
88|progression by investigators was audited with the
89|use of the method of the Pharmaceutical Re-
90|search and Manufacturers Association26 in a sam-
91|ple of 202 randomly selected patients with blind-
92|ed central review.
93|Prespecified secondary end points were the
94|time to the next "skeletal-related event" (described
95|here as a "symptomatic skeletal event," which
96|was defined as a clinical or pathological frac-
97|ture, spinal-cord compression, palliative radia-
98|tion to bone, or surgery involving bone), time to
99|progression with respect to prostate-specific
100|antigen (PSA) level on the basis of Prostate Can-
101|cer Working Group 2 criteria,25 time to the next
102|therapy for prostate cancer, time to initiation of
103|chemotherapy, and time to pain progression.

4|Pain progression was defined as an increase of
5|at least 30% from baseline in the worst pain
6|category on the Brief Pain Inventory-Short Form
7|as observed at two consecutive evaluations per-
8|formed at least 4 weeks apart.
9|Assessments
10|Efficacy assessments included sequential radio-
11|graphic imaging to assess radiographic progres-
12|sion-free survival (CT or MRI and bone scan-
13|ning) performed every 4 months, starting at
14|week 16. PSA levels were measured at baseline,
15|monthly in the first year, and then every 2 months
16|until end-of-trial treatment. Patients underwent
17|serial monitoring of vital signs, serum hemato-
18|logic and chemical findings, liver-function tests,
19|and serum testosterone levels. Adverse events
20|were graded with the use of the Common Termi-
21|nology Criteria for Adverse Events of the Na-
22|tional Cancer Institute, version 4.0.
23|Statistical Analysis
24|The overall level of significance was 0.05, with
25|allocation between the two primary end points
26|of overall survival (0.049) and radiographic
27|progression-free survival (0.001) (Table S2 in
28|the Supplementary Appendix). For overall sur-
29|vival, 852 events were required at the final
30|analysis to detect a hazard ratio of 0.81 at a
31|two-tailed significance level of 0.049, with a
32|statistical power of 85%. An analysis of radio-
33|graphic progression-free survival was planned
34|when 565 progressions or deaths had been ob-
35|served, which would provide a statistical power
36|of 94% to detect a hazard ratio of 0.667 at a
37|two-tailed significance level of 0.001. Two in-
38|terim analyses were included (Table S2 in the
39|Supplementary Appendix). The overall survival
40|analyses incorporated the group sequential de-
41|sign with an alpha spending function that was
42|calculated as Wang-Tsiatis power boundaries
43|of shape parameter 0.2 (which shape the prob-
44|ability distribution). Secondary end points were
45|tested with the use of the Hochberg test proce-
46|dure to control the familywise type I error rate.
47|The primary statistical method of comparison
48|for time-to-event end points was the stratified
49|log-rank test, according to the stratification
50|factors. The Cox proportional-hazards model
51|was used to estimate the hazard ratio and its
52|associated 95% confidence interval.
53|Results
54|Patients and Treatments
55|A total of 1199 patients underwent randomiza-
56|tion from February 12, 2013, through December
57|11, 2014. Of these patients, 597 were assigned to
58|the abiraterone group and 602 to the placebo
59|group (Fig. S1 in the Supplementary Appendix).
60|The baseline demographic and disease charac-
61|teristics were well balanced between the two
62|groups (Table S3 in the Supplementary Appen-
63|dix). The results presented here are based on the
64|clinical cutoff date of October 31, 2016, for the
65|first interim analysis of overall survival, at which
66|time 406 deaths and 593 radiographic progres-
67|sions or deaths had occurred. At a median follow-
68|up of 30.4 months, the median time that the
69|patients received the intervention was 24 months
70|in the abiraterone group and 14 months in the
71|placebo group. As a result of the findings at the
72|time of the interim analysis, the independent data
73|and safety monitoring committee unanimously
74|recommended on January 12, 2017, that the trial
75|be unblinded to allow crossover among the pa-
76|tients in the placebo group to receive abiraterone.
77|End Points
78|Overall Survival
79|The first interim analysis was performed after
80|406 deaths (48% of the 852 deaths that were
81|included in the final analysis) and a median
82|follow-up of 30.4 months. Of these deaths, 169 of
83|597 (28%) occurred in the abiraterone group and
84|237 of 602 (39%) in the placebo group. The over-
85|all rate of survival at 3 years was 66% in the
86|abiraterone group and 49% in the placebo group
87|(Fig. 1A). The rate of death from any cause was
88|28% in the abiraterone group and 39% in the
89|placebo group (Table S4 in the Supplementary
90|Appendix). The relative risk of death was 38%
91|lower in the abiraterone group than in the pla-
92|cebo group (hazard ratio, 0.62; 95% confidence
93|interval [CI], 0.51 to 0.76; P<0.001). The treatment
94|effect of abiraterone on overall survival was consis-
95|tently favorable across nearly all prespecified sub-
96|groups (Fig. S2 in the Supplementary Appendix).
97|Radiographic Progression-free Survival
98|At the time of the analysis, the median progression-
99|free survival was 33.0 months in the abiraterone
100|group and 14.8 months in the placebo group

23|Safety
24|Grade 3 or 4 adverse events were reported in
25|63% of the patients in the abiraterone group and
26|in 48% of those in the placebo group (Table 2).
27|The numbers of patients with serious adverse
28|events were similar in the two groups. The fre-
29|quency of adverse events leading to treatment
30|discontinuation was 12% in the abiraterone group
31|and 10% in the placebo group (Table S6 in the
32|Supplementary Appendix). Adverse events that
33|led to a dose modification or interruption were
34|reported in 32% of the patients in the abiraterone
35|group and in 17% of those in the placebo group.
36|Grade 3 mineralocorticoid-related toxic effects
37|of special interest, including hypertension and
38|hypokalemia, occurred at a higher frequency in
39|the abiraterone group than in the placebo group;
40|rates of grade 3 and grade 4 hypertension were
41|20% and 0%, respectively, in the abiraterone
42|group and 10% and 0.2%, respectively, in the
43|placebo group, with corresponding rates of hypo-
44|kalemia of 10% and 0.8% in the abiraterone
45|group and of 1% and 0.2% in the placebo group
46|(Table 2).
47|Discussion
48|In this phase 3 trial involving men with high-
49|risk, newly diagnosed, metastatic, castration-
50|sensitive prostate cancer, the rate of overall
51|survival was significantly higher among those
52|who received androgen-deprivation therapy plus
53|abiraterone and prednisone than among those
54|who received androgen-deprivation therapy plus
55|placebos, with a 38% lower relative risk of death
56|(hazard ratio, 0.62) in the abiraterone group.
57|The addition of abiraterone plus prednisone to
58|androgen-deprivation therapy also significantly
59|prolonged radiographic progression-free survival
60|(hazard ratio, 0.47) and all secondary end points.
61|Since the between-group difference for overall
62|survival was significant at the time of the first
63|interim analysis and unblinding of the trial, this
64|analysis is considered to be final.

Our data support the hypoth- 9|esis that more effective inhibition of androgen- 10|receptor signaling as a component of the initial 11|systemic therapy in patients with castration- 12|sensitive prostate cancer leads to improved out- 13|comes. The clinical benefit that we observed con- 14|trasts with that from the many previous attempts 15|with castration and first-generation androgen- 16|receptor inhibitors,27,28 which showed only a 17|small improvement with a combined androgen- 18|blockade approach,29 presumably owing to the 19|lower potency and partial agonist activity of 20|these drugs. Several other ongoing randomized, 21|phase 3 trials in this patient population are ex- 22|amining androgen receptor-signaling combina- 23|tion therapies with androgen-deprivation ther 24|apy (Table S7 in the Supplementary Appendix) 25|and are exploring whether these treatments can 26|be added to androgen-deprivation therapy plus 27|docetaxel in patients with metastatic, castration- 28|sensitive prostate cancer. The assessment of effi- 29|cacy of subsequent therapies, including the types 30|of disease progression in patients who were re- 31|ceiving treatment, will require more long-term 32|analysis. 33|Men with newly diagnosed, metastatic, castra- 34|tion-sensitive prostate cancer can have variable 35|outcomes, so we purposely enrolled those who 36|were considered to have at least two high-risk 37|prognostic features (e.g., a Gleason score of ≥8, 38|the presence of ≥3 bone lesions, or the presence 39|of measurable visceral metastasis),30-33 all of which 40|are associated with poor survival. In addition, 41|50% of the patients had symptomatic disease at 42|baseline. The patient population appears to be 43|similar to high-burden disease populations in 44|the three randomized trials that evaluated andro- 45|gen-deprivation therapy plus docetaxel,3,5,7 since 46|the outcomes in the control groups were similar 47|across those studies. After a median follow-up 48|of 7 years in GETUG-15, a nonsignificant 22% 49|reduction in the relative risk of death was ob- 50|served in patients with high-volume disease.8 A 51|significant 27% reduction in the relative risk of 52|death (and a reduction of 37% in patients with 53|high-volume disease) with androgen-deprivation 54|therapy plus docetaxel was observed after a 53.7- 55|month follow-up (approximately 50% of deaths) 56|in CHAARTED.6 In STAMPEDE, a significant 24% 57|risk reduction in death was observed among pa- 58|tients with metastatic, castration-sensitive pros- 59|tate cancer.7 (The STAMPEDE investigators now 60|report in the Journal the results of another trial 61|of abiraterone plus prednisone in men with local 62|ly advanced or metastatic prostate cancer.34) In 63|our trial, the efficacy of abiraterone, with a 38% 64|reduction in the risk of death among patients 65|who had not received previous treatment for 66|metastatic disease, compares favorably with pre- 67|vious findings. questions.wording: Was the allocation sequence random?
questions.official_guidance: Answer ‘Yes’ if a random component was used in the sequence generation process. Examples include computer-generated random numbers; reference to a random number table; coin tossing; shuffling cards or envelopes; throwing dice; or drawing lots. Answer ‘No’ if no random element was used in generating the allocation sequence or the sequence is predictable. Answer ‘No information’ if the only information about randomization methods is a statement that the study is randomized.
questions.source_locator: Full guidance p. 17, Box 4, signalling question 1.1
questions.bias_construct: Whether a random component was used to generate the allocation sequence.
questions.decision_rule: Answer yes when a random component was used; answer no when no random element was used or the sequence is predictable. A statement that the study is randomized alone supports no_information.
evidence_needed: The sequence-generation method, such as computer random numbers, a random number table, coin tossing, or minimization with a random element.
questions.no_information_rule: Answer no_information when the only information about randomization methods is that the study is randomized. Do not turn missing reporting into proof that the sequence was non-random.

answer_anchors.text: A random component was used in sequence generation.
No random element was used, or the sequence was predictable.
The report only states that the study is randomized.

considerations: Minimization should generally be considered random when it includes a random element.

Sequence generation asks how the allocation sequence was produced; concealment asks whether forthcoming assignments were hidden before enrolment and assignment; baseline imbalance asks whether the resulting groups suggest a randomization problem. Evidence for one does not answer the others.
The baseline-imbalance answer must not change this answer.

evidence.quote:
n engl j med 377;4 nejm.org July 27, 2017
355
Abiraterone plus Prednisone in Prostate Cancer
Pain progression was defined as an increase of
at least 30% from baseline in the worst pain
category on the Brief Pain Inventory-Short Form
as observed at two consecutive evaluations per-
formed at least 4 weeks apart.
Assessments
Efficacy assessments included sequential radio-
graphic imaging to assess radiographic progres-
sion-free survival (CT or MRI and bone scan-
ning) performed every 4 months, starting at
week 16. PSA levels were measured at baseline,
monthly in the first year, and then every 2 months
until end-of-trial treatment. Patients underwent
serial monitoring of vital signs, serum hemato-
logic and chemical findings, liver-function tests,
and serum testosterone levels. Adverse events
were graded with the use of the Common Termi-
nology Criteria for Adverse Events of the Na-
tional Cancer Institute, version 4.0.
Statistical Analysis
The overall level of significance was 0.05, with
allocation between the two primary end points
of overall survival (0.049) and radiographic
progression-free survival (0.001) (Table S2 in
the Supplementary Appendix). For overall sur-
vival, 852 events were required at the final
analysis to detect a hazard ratio of 0.81 at a
two-tailed significance level of 0.049, with a
statistical power of 85%. An analysis of radio-
graphic progression-free survival was planned
when 565 progressions or deaths had been ob-
served, which would provide a statistical power
of 94% to detect a hazard ratio of 0.667 at a
two-tailed significance level of 0.001. Two in-
terim analyses were included (Table S2 in the
Supplementary Appendix). The overall survival
analyses incorporated the group sequential de-
sign with an alpha spending function that was
calculated as Wang-Tsiatis power boundaries
of shape parameter 0.2 (which shape the prob-
ability distribution). Secondary end points were
tested with the use of the Hochberg test proce-
dure to control the familywise type I error rate.
The primary statistical method of comparison
for time-to-event end points was the stratified
log-rank test, according to the stratification
factors. The Cox proportional-hazards model
was used to estimate the hazard ratio and its
associated 95% confidence interval.
Results
Patients and Treatments
A total of 1199 patients underwent randomiza-
tion from February 12, 2013, through December
11, 2014. Of these patients, 597 were assigned to
the abiraterone group and 602 to the placebo
group (Fig. S1 in the Supplementary Appendix).
The baseline demographic and disease charac-
teristics were well balanced between the two
groups (Table S3 in the Supplementary Appen-
dix). The results presented here are based on the
clinical cutoff date of October 31, 2016, for the
first interim analysis of overall survival, at which
time 406 deaths and 593 radiographic progres-
sions or deaths had occurred. At a median follow-
up of 30.4 months, the median time that the
patients received the intervention was 24 months
in the abiraterone group and 14 months in the
placebo group. As a result of the findings at the
time of the interim analysis, the independent data
and safety monitoring committee unanimously
recommended on January 12, 2017, that the trial
be unblinded to allow crossover among the pa-
tients in the placebo group to receive abiraterone.
End Points
Overall Survival
The first interim analysis was performed after
406 deaths (48% of the 852 deaths that were
included in the final analysis) and a median
follow-up of 30.4 months. Of these deaths, 169 of
597 (28%) occurred in the abiraterone group and
237 of 602 (39%) in the placebo group. The over-
all rate of survival at 3 years was 66% in the
abiraterone group and 49% in the placebo group
(Fig. 1A). The rate of death from any cause was
28% in the abiraterone group and 39% in the
placebo group (Table S4 in the Supplementary
Appendix). The relative risk of death was 38%
lower in the abiraterone group than in the pla-
cebo group (hazard ratio, 0.62; 95% confidence
interval [CI], 0.51 to 0.76; P<0.001). The treatment
effect of abiraterone on overall survival was consis-
tently favorable across nearly all prespecified sub-
groups (Fig. S2 in the Supplementary Appendix).
Radiographic Progression-free Survival
At the time of the analysis, the median progression-
free survival was 33.0 months in the abiraterone
group and 14.8 months in the placebo group

response_framework.firm_evidence_rule: The definitive versions (‘Yes’ and ‘No’) would typically imply that firm evidence is available in relation to the signalling question.
response_framework.probable_judgment_rule: The ‘Probably’ versions would typically imply that a judgement has been made. ‘Yes’ and ‘Probably yes’ have the same implications for risk of bias, as do ‘No’ and ‘Probably no’.
response_framework.no_information_rule: Use ‘No information’ only when both (i) insufficient details are reported to permit a response of ‘Probably yes’ or ‘Probably no’, and (ii) in the absence of these details it would be unreasonable to respond ‘Probably yes’ or ‘Probably no’ in the circumstances of the trial.
response_framework.independence_rule: Signalling questions should be answered independently: the answer to one question should not affect answers to other questions in the same or other domains other than through determining which subsequent questions are answered.
response_framework.quotation_rule: Brief direct quotations from the text of the study report should be used whenever possible to support the answer.

traps: A no-hit search describes one lexical query, not scientific absence.
A planned method does not prove conduct; a time origin or analysis population does not prove complete follow-up or equal assessment.
An endpoint label or definition does not prove objectivity, blinding, prespecification, or no alternative analyses.
A treatment assignment or visibly different intervention does not by itself prove that participants or personnel knew the assignment.
Different treatment or visit schedules do not by themselves prove that outcome measurement differed between groups.
Stratification does not prove allocation concealment.
data.completion_rule: Ground each active proposition and its uncertainty in inspected Evidence or bounded discovery for unresolved premises. Supply every question activated by the submitted answer path with an Evidence use, scoped absence receipt, or limitation. Inactive extras are ignored.

sections.excerpt: Answer ‘Yes’ if the trial used any form of remote or centrally administered method to allocate interventions to participants, where the process of allocation is controlled by an external unit or organization, independent of the enrolment personnel. Answer ‘Yes’ if envelopes or drug containers were used appropriately. Answer ‘No’ if there is reason to suspect that the enrolling investigator or the participant had knowledge of the forthcoming allocation.

sections.source_locator: Full guidance pp. 17-18, Box 4, signalling question 1.3
sections.excerpt: Note that differences that are compatible with chance do not lead to a risk of bias. Answer ‘No’ if no imbalances are apparent or if any observed imbalances are compatible with chance. Answer ‘Yes’ if there are imbalances that indicate problems with the randomization process, including substantial differences between intervention group sizes, a substantial excess in statistically significant differences beyond that expected by chance, or imbalance in one or more key prognostic factors very unlikely to be due to chance. Answer ‘No information’ when there is no useful baseline information available.

questions.bias_construct: Whether the allocation sequence was concealed until participants were enrolled and assigned.
considerations: Allocation concealment concerns the process before assignment, not blinding after assignment.

Keep concealment separate from sequence generation (how the sequence was made) and baseline imbalance (what the randomized groups look like). A random sequence or balanced baseline table does not establish concealment.
The reported sequence-generation method does not establish concealment.

questions.decision_rule: Answer yes for remote or centrally administered allocation independent of enrolment personnel, or appropriately used opaque sequentially numbered sealed envelopes or identical sequentially numbered drug containers. evidence_needed: The method used before assignment and who controlled it; for envelopes or containers, capture the details that make them tamper-resistant and irreversible before assignment.
questions.no_information_rule: Answer no_information when the report does not provide enough information to assess concealment; do not infer concealment from central registration or a sequence number alone.

item.text: The protocol describes permuted-block randomization and a centralized IWRS, and says investigators did not receive the randomization codes. The baseline table shows broadly similar groups, with no large prognostic imbalance apparent. I’ll record those findings for Domain 1 and then proceed through the remaining Domains in order.

answers.justification: The protocol states that allocation used permuted block randomization, a random sequence method. It also describes a 1:1 allocation stratified by country, visceral disease, and ECOG status.

The protocol states that randomization was handled through a centralized Interactive Web Response System after eligibility was verified, and that investigators were not provided the randomization codes. This supports concealment of assignments until enrollment and assignment.

The baseline table shows similar group sizes and comparable distributions for key prognostic characteristics: Gleason score at least 8 was 98% versus 97%, at least three bone metastases 98.2% versus 97.2%, and high-risk status 96% versus 95%. Median ages were 68 and 67 years. No substantial imbalance suggesting a randomization problem is apparent.
unknowns: Some baseline characteristics have missing observations, and the article does not report a formal test for overall baseline imbalance.

evidence.quote:
n engl j med 377;4 nejm.org July 27, 2017
355
Abiraterone plus Prednisone in Prostate Cancer
Pain progression was defined as an increase of
at least 30% from baseline in the worst pain
category on the Brief Pain Inventory-Short Form
as observed at two consecutive evaluations per-
formed at least 4 weeks apart.
Assessments
Efficacy assessments included sequential radio-
graphic imaging to assess radiographic progres-
sion-free survival (CT or MRI and bone scan-
ning) performed every 4 months, starting at
week 16. PSA levels were measured at baseline,
monthly in the first year, and then every 2 months
until end-of-trial treatment. Patients underwent
serial monitoring of vital signs, serum hemato-
logic and chemical findings, liver-function tests,
and serum testosterone levels. Adverse events
were graded with the use of the Common Termi-
nology Criteria for Adverse Events of the Na-
tional Cancer Institute, version 4.0.
Statistical Analysis
The overall level of significance was 0.05, with
allocation between the two primary end points
of overall survival (0.049) and radiographic
progression-free survival (0.001) (Table S2 in
the Supplementary Appendix). For overall sur-
vival, 852 events were required at the final
analysis to detect a hazard ratio of 0.81 at a
two-tailed significance level of 0.049, with a
statistical power of 85%. An analysis of radio-
graphic progression-free survival was planned
when 565 progressions or deaths had been ob-
served, which would provide a statistical power
of 94% to detect a hazard ratio of 0.667 at a
two-tailed significance level of 0.001. Two in-
terim analyses were included (Table S2 in the
Supplementary Appendix). The overall survival
analyses incorporated the group sequential de-
sign with an alpha spending function that was
calculated as Wang-Tsiatis power boundaries
of shape parameter 0.2 (which shape the prob-
ability distribution). Secondary end points were
tested with the use of the Hochberg test proce-
dure to control the familywise type I error rate.
The primary statistical method of comparison
for time-to-event end points was the stratified
log-rank test, according to the stratification
factors. The Cox proportional-hazards model
was used to estimate the hazard ratio and its
associated 95% confidence interval.
Results
Patients and Treatments
A total of 1199 patients underwent randomiza-
tion from February 12, 2013, through December
11, 2014. Of these patients, 597 were assigned to
the abiraterone group and 602 to the placebo
group (Fig. S1 in the Supplementary Appendix).
The baseline demographic and disease charac-
teristics were well balanced between the two
groups (Table S3 in the Supplementary Appen-
dix). The results presented here are based on the
clinical cutoff date of October 31, 2016, for the
first interim analysis of overall survival, at which
time 406 deaths and 593 radiographic progres-
sions or deaths had occurred. At a median follow-
up of 30.4 months, the median time that the
patients received the intervention was 24 months
in the abiraterone group and 14 months in the
placebo group. As a result of the findings at the
time of the interim analysis, the independent data
and safety monitoring committee unanimously
recommended on January 12, 2017, that the trial
be unblinded to allow crossover among the pa-
tients in the placebo group to receive abiraterone.
End Points
Overall Survival
The first interim analysis was performed after
406 deaths (48% of the 852 deaths that were
included in the final analysis) and a median
follow-up of 30.4 months. Of these deaths, 169 of
597 (28%) occurred in the abiraterone group and
237 of 602 (39%) in the placebo group. The over-
all rate of survival at 3 years was 66% in the
abiraterone group and 49% in the placebo group
(Fig. 1A). The rate of death from any cause was
28% in the abiraterone group and 39% in the
placebo group (Table S4 in the Supplementary
Appendix). The relative risk of death was 38%
lower in the abiraterone group than in the pla-
cebo group (hazard ratio, 0.62; 95% confidence
interval [CI], 0.51 to 0.76; P<0.001). The treatment
effect of abiraterone on overall survival was consis-
tently favorable across nearly all prespecified sub-
groups (Fig. S2 in the Supplementary Appendix).
Radiographic Progression-free Survival
At the time of the analysis, the median progression-
free survival was 33.0 months in the abiraterone
group and 14.8 months in the placebo group

response_framework.firm_evidence_rule: The definitive versions (‘Yes’ and ‘No’) would typically imply that firm evidence is available in relation to the signalling question.
response_framework.probable_judgment_rule: The ‘Probably’ versions would typically imply that a judgement has been made. ‘Yes’ and ‘Probably yes’ have the same implications for risk of bias, as do ‘No’ and ‘Probably no’.
response_framework.no_information_rule: Use ‘No information’ only when both (i) insufficient details are reported to permit a response of ‘Probably yes’ or ‘Probably no’, and (ii) in the absence of these details it would be unreasonable to respond ‘Probably yes’ or ‘Probably no’ in the circumstances of the trial.
response_framework.independence_rule: Signalling questions should be answered independently: the answer to one question should not affect answers to other questions in the same or other domains other than through determining which subsequent questions are answered.
response_framework.quotation_rule: Brief direct quotations from the text of the study report should be used whenever possible to support the answer.

Answer no or probably no when no such deviation occurred, including ordinary non-adherence outside the trial context, protocol-consistent changes, and protocol-permitted subsequent care after progression.
evidence_needed: Evidence linking the deviation to recruitment, engagement, or trial personnel and showing it was inconsistent with the protocol.
invalid_shortcuts: unequal post-progression treatment without evidence that it was prohibited and trial-context-caused
a protocol deviation without its cause
discontinuation or crossover without protocol and cause evidence
questions.no_information_rule: Use no_information when reported details are insufficient and trial circumstances do not support a reasonable probable judgment about trial-context-caused deviations.
questions.official_guidance: Answer ‘Yes’ or ‘Probably yes’ only if there is evidence, or strong reason to believe, that the trial context led to failure to implement the protocol interventions or to implementation of interventions not allowed by the protocol. Answer ‘No’ or ‘Probably no’ if there were changes from assigned intervention that are inconsistent with the trial protocol, such as non-adherence to intervention, but these are consistent with what could occur outside the trial context. The answer ‘No information’ may be appropriate.

considerations: Balance refers to the deviations identified in 2.3 and their potential effect, not to baseline group sizes.

considerations: The question is about effect of assignment, so grouping must follow randomized assignment.

43|METHODS
44|In this double-blind, placebo-controlled, phase 3 trial, we randomly assigned 1199 pa-
45|tients to receive either androgen-deprivation therapy plus abiraterone acetate (1000 mg
46|daily, given once daily as four 250-mg tablets) plus prednisone (5 mg daily) (the
47|abiraterone group) or androgen-deprivation therapy plus dual placebos (the placebo
48|group). The two primary end points were overall survival and radiographic progression-
49|free survival.
50|RESULTS
51|After a median follow-up of 30.4 months at a planned interim analysis (after 406 pa-
52|tients had died), the median overall survival was significantly longer in the abiraterone
53|group than in the placebo group (not reached vs. 34.7 months) (hazard ratio for death,
54|0.62; 95% confidence interval [CI], 0.51 to 0.76; P<0.001). The median length of radio-
55|graphic progression-free survival was 33.0 months in the abiraterone group and 14.8
56|months in the placebo group (hazard ratio for disease progression or death, 0.47; 95%
57|CI, 0.39 to 0.55; P<0.001). Significantly better outcomes in all secondary end points
58|were observed in the abiraterone group, including the time until pain progression, next
59|subsequent therapy for prostate cancer, initiation of chemotherapy, and prostate-
60|specific antigen progression (P<0.001 for all comparisons), along with next symptom-
61|atic skeletal events (P = 0.009). These findings led to the unanimous recommendation
62|by the independent data and safety monitoring committee that the trial be unblinded
63|and crossover be allowed for patients in the placebo group to receive abiraterone. Rates
64|of grade 3 hypertension and hypokalemia were higher in the abiraterone group.
65|CONCLUSIONS
66|The addition of abiraterone acetate and prednisone to androgen-deprivation therapy
67|significantly increased overall survival and radiographic progression-free survival in
68|men with newly diagnosed, metastatic, castration-sensitive prostate cancer. (Funded
69|by Janssen Research and Development; LATITUDE ClinicalTrials.gov number,
70|NCT01715285.)

evidence_needed: For yes or probably yes, actual outcome-availability evidence can be comparable observed-outcome counts, arm-specific loss-to-follow-up or censoring accounting, or an explicit complete/nearly-complete ascertainment statement.

Compare the approved outcome/time point across participant-flow and outcome-data passages. For each comparable arm or unit distinguish the randomized denominator, outcome-observed count, analysed count, imputed count, post-randomization excluded count, and event count. An event count is a numerator, not an outcome-observed count; an analysis denominator is not necessarily an outcome-observed count. Keep outcome availability separate from mitigation quality: a sensitivity analysis or imputation does not change the observed count, and observed cannot be inferred as analysed minus imputed unless the source establishes the same population, time window, and mutually exclusive counts.

n engl j med 377;4 nejm.org July 27, 2017
355
Abiraterone plus Prednisone in Prostate Cancer
Pain progression was defined as an increase of
at least 30% from baseline in the worst pain
category on the Brief Pain Inventory-Short Form
as observed at two consecutive evaluations per-
formed at least 4 weeks apart.
Assessments
Efficacy assessments included sequential radio-
graphic imaging to assess radiographic progres-
sion-free survival (CT or MRI and bone scan-
ning) performed every 4 months, starting at
week 16. PSA levels were measured at baseline,
monthly in the first year, and then every 2 months
until end-of-trial treatment. Patients underwent
serial monitoring of vital signs, serum hemato-
logic and chemical findings, liver-function tests,
and serum testosterone levels. Adverse events
were graded with the use of the Common Termi-
nology Criteria for Adverse Events of the Na-
tional Cancer Institute, version 4.0.
Statistical Analysis
The overall level of significance was 0.05, with
allocation between the two primary end points
of overall survival (0.049) and radiographic
progression-free survival (0.001) (Table S2 in
the Supplementary Appendix). For overall sur-
vival, 852 events were required at the final
analysis to detect a hazard ratio of 0.81 at a
two-tailed significance level of 0.049, with a
statistical power of 85%. An analysis of radio-
graphic progression-free survival was planned
when 565 progressions or deaths had been ob-
served, which would provide a statistical power
of 94% to detect a hazard ratio of 0.667 at a
two-tailed significance level of 0.001. Two in-
terim analyses were included (Table S2 in the
Supplementary Appendix). The overall survival
analyses incorporated the group sequential de-
sign with an alpha spending function that was
calculated as Wang-Tsiatis power boundaries
of shape parameter 0.2 (which shape the prob-
ability distribution). Secondary end points were
tested with the use of the Hochberg test proce-
dure to control the familywise type I error rate.
The primary statistical method of comparison
for time-to-event end points was the stratified
log-rank test, according to the stratification
factors. The Cox proportional-hazards model
was used to estimate the hazard ratio and its
associated 95% confidence interval.
Results
Patients and Treatments
A total of 1199 patients underwent randomiza-
tion from February 12, 2013, through December
11, 2014. Of these patients, 597 were assigned to
the abiraterone group and 602 to the placebo
group (Fig. S1 in the Supplementary Appendix).
The baseline demographic and disease charac-
teristics were well balanced between the two
groups (Table S3 in the Supplementary Appen-
dix). The results presented here are based on the
clinical cutoff date of October 31, 2016, for the
first interim analysis of overall survival, at which
time 406 deaths and 593 radiographic progres-
sions or deaths had occurred. At a median follow-
up of 30.4 months, the median time that the
patients received the intervention was 24 months
in the abiraterone group and 14 months in the
placebo group. As a result of the findings at the
time of the interim analysis, the independent data
and safety monitoring committee unanimously
recommended on January 12, 2017, that the trial
be unblinded to allow crossover among the pa-
tients in the placebo group to receive abiraterone.
End Points
Overall Survival
The first interim analysis was performed after
406 deaths (48% of the 852 deaths that were
included in the final analysis) and a median
follow-up of 30.4 months. Of these deaths, 169 of
597 (28%) occurred in the abiraterone group and
237 of 602 (39%) in the placebo group. The over-
all rate of survival at 3 years was 66% in the
abiraterone group and 49% in the placebo group
(Fig. 1A). The rate of death from any cause was
28% in the abiraterone group and 39% in the
placebo group (Table S4 in the Supplementary
Appendix). The relative risk of death was 38%
lower in the abiraterone group than in the pla-
cebo group (hazard ratio, 0.62; 95% confidence
interval [CI], 0.51 to 0.76; P<0.001). The treatment
effect of abiraterone on overall survival was consis-
tently favorable across nearly all prespecified sub-
groups (Fig. S2 in the Supplementary Appendix).
Radiographic Progression-free Survival
At the time of the analysis, the median progression-
free survival was 33.0 months in the abiraterone
group and 14.8 months in the placebo group

response_framework.firm_evidence_rule: The definitive versions (‘Yes’ and ‘No’) would typically imply that firm evidence is available in relation to the signalling question.
response_framework.probable_judgment_rule: The ‘Probably’ versions would typically imply that a judgement has been made. ‘Yes’ and ‘Probably yes’ have the same implications for risk of bias, as do ‘No’ and ‘Probably no’.
response_framework.no_information_rule: Use ‘No information’ only when both (i) insufficient details are reported to permit a response of ‘Probably yes’ or ‘Probably no’, and (ii) in the absence of these details it would be unreasonable to respond ‘Probably yes’ or ‘Probably no’ in the circumstances of the trial.
response_framework.independence_rule: Signalling questions should be answered independently: the answer to one question should not affect answers to other questions in the same or other domains other than through determining which subsequent questions are answered.
response_framework.quotation_rule: Brief direct quotations from the text of the study report should be used whenever possible to support the answer.

questions.wording: Was the method of measuring the outcome inappropriate?
questions.official_guidance: Answer ‘Yes’ or ‘Probably yes’ if the method of measuring the outcome is inappropriate, for example because it is unlikely to be sensitive to plausible intervention effects or the measurement instrument has been demonstrated to have poor validity.
questions.source_locator: Full guidance p. 54, Box 10, signalling question 4.1
questions.bias_construct: Whether the method of measuring the outcome was inappropriate for the outcome, including validity and sensitivity to plausible intervention effects.
questions.decision_rule: Answer yes or probably yes when the method is unlikely to be sensitive to plausible intervention effects or the instrument has demonstrated poor validity. Validity and sensitivity are distinct from detection opportunity, assessor identity or awareness, and whether knowledge influenced assessment. Do not assess whether choosing the outcome itself was sensible.
evidence_needed: The measurement method's sensitivity to plausible effects and evidence of instrument validity for this outcome.

For a mixed objective and subjective composite, inspect each component that can determine the approved event; objective components do not establish validity or influence conclusions for a subjective component.
questions.no_information_rule: Use no_information when appropriateness of the measurement method cannot be determined.

answer_anchors.text: The measurement method is unsuitable, insensitive, or poorly valid for this outcome.
The measurement method is appropriate for this outcome.

considerations: For pre-specified outcomes the answer will usually be no or probably no.

Measurement susceptibility concerns whether the method can validly and sensitively measure this outcome. It is distinct from assessor awareness, detection opportunity, and whether knowledge of intervention likely influenced assessment.

A standardized instrument can still involve judgment in elicitation, attribution, grading, or assessment. Preserve component-specific Evidence and uncertainty for mixed objective and subjective components.

evidence.quote:
n engl j med 377;4 nejm.org July 27, 2017
355
Abiraterone plus Prednisone in Prostate Cancer
Pain progression was defined as an increase of
at least 30% from baseline in the worst pain
category on the Brief Pain Inventory-Short Form
as observed at two consecutive evaluations per-
formed at least 4 weeks apart.
Assessments
Efficacy assessments included sequential radio-
graphic imaging to assess radiographic progres-
sion-free survival (CT or MRI and bone scan-
ning) performed every 4 months, starting at
week 16. PSA levels were measured at baseline,
monthly in the first year, and then every 2 months
until end-of-trial treatment. Patients underwent
serial monitoring of vital signs, serum hemato-
logic and chemical findings, liver-function tests,
and serum testosterone levels. Adverse events
were graded with the use of the Common Termi-
nology Criteria for Adverse Events of the Na-
tional Cancer Institute, version 4.0.
Statistical Analysis
The overall level of significance was 0.05, with
allocation between the two primary end points
of overall survival (0.049) and radiographic
progression-free survival (0.001) (Table S2 in
the Supplementary Appendix). For overall sur-
vival, 852 events were required at the final
analysis to detect a hazard ratio of 0.81 at a
two-tailed significance level of 0.049, with a
statistical power of 85%. An analysis of radio-
graphic progression-free survival was planned
when 565 progressions or deaths had been ob-
served, which would provide a statistical power
of 94% to detect a hazard ratio of 0.667 at a
two-tailed significance level of 0.001. Two in-
terim analyses were included (Table S2 in the
Supplementary Appendix). The overall survival
analyses incorporated the group sequential de-
sign with an alpha spending function that was
calculated as Wang-Tsiatis power boundaries
of shape parameter 0.2 (which shape the prob-
ability distribution). Secondary end points were
tested with the use of the Hochberg test proce-
dure to control the familywise type I error rate.
The primary statistical method of comparison
for time-to-event end points was the stratified
log-rank test, according to the stratification
factors. The Cox proportional-hazards model
was used to estimate the hazard ratio and its
associated 95% confidence interval.
Results
Patients and Treatments
A total of 1199 patients underwent randomiza-
tion from February 12, 2013, through December
11, 2014. Of these patients, 597 were assigned to
the abiraterone group and 602 to the placebo
group (Fig. S1 in the Supplementary Appendix).
The baseline demographic and disease charac-
teristics were well balanced between the two
groups (Table S3 in the Supplementary Appen-
dix). The results presented here are based on the
clinical cutoff date of October 31, 2016, for the
first interim analysis of overall survival, at which
time 406 deaths and 593 radiographic progres-
sions or deaths had occurred. At a median follow-
up of 30.4 months, the median time that the
patients received the intervention was 24 months
in the abiraterone group and 14 months in the
placebo group. As a result of the findings at the
time of the interim analysis, the independent data
and safety monitoring committee unanimously
recommended on January 12, 2017, that the trial
be unblinded to allow crossover among the pa-
tients in the placebo group to receive abiraterone.
End Points
Overall Survival
The first interim analysis was performed after
406 deaths (48% of the 852 deaths that were
included in the final analysis) and a median
follow-up of 30.4 months. Of these deaths, 169 of
597 (28%) occurred in the abiraterone group and
237 of 602 (39%) in the placebo group. The over-
all rate of survival at 3 years was 66% in the
abiraterone group and 49% in the placebo group
(Fig. 1A). The rate of death from any cause was
28% in the abiraterone group and 39% in the
placebo group (Table S4 in the Supplementary
Appendix). The relative risk of death was 38%
lower in the abiraterone group than in the pla-
cebo group (hazard ratio, 0.62; 95% confidence
interval [CI], 0.51 to 0.76; P<0.001). The treatment
effect of abiraterone on overall survival was consis-
tently favorable across nearly all prespecified sub-
groups (Fig. S2 in the Supplementary Appendix).
Radiographic Progression-free Survival
At the time of the analysis, the median progression-
free survival was 33.0 months in the abiraterone
group and 14.8 months in the placebo group

response_framework.firm_evidence_rule: The definitive versions (‘Yes’ and ‘No’) would typically imply that firm evidence is available in relation to the signalling question.
response_framework.probable_judgment_rule: The ‘Probably’ versions would typically imply that a judgement has been made. ‘Yes’ and ‘Probably yes’ have the same implications for risk of bias, as do ‘No’ and ‘Probably no’.
response_framework.no_information_rule: Use ‘No information’ only when both (i) insufficient details are reported to permit a response of ‘Probably yes’ or ‘Probably no’, and (ii) in the absence of these details it would be unreasonable to respond ‘Probably yes’ or ‘Probably no’ in the circumstances of the trial.
response_framework.independence_rule: Signalling questions should be answered independently: the answer to one question should not affect answers to other questions in the same or other domains other than through determining which subsequent questions are answered.
response_framework.quotation_rule: Brief direct quotations from the text of the study report should be used whenever possible to support the answer.

traps: A no-hit search describes one lexical query, not scientific absence.
A planned method does not prove conduct; a time origin or analysis population does not prove complete follow-up or equal assessment.
An endpoint label or definition does not prove objectivity, blinding, prespecification, or no alternative analyses.
A treatment assignment or visibly different intervention does not by itself prove that participants or personnel knew the assignment.
Different treatment or visit schedules do not by themselves prove that outcome measurement differed between groups.
Stratification does not prove allocation concealment.

questions.bias_construct: Whether knowledge of intervention likely influenced outcome assessment. Require evidence or strong beliefs plus a judgement opportunity; awareness alone does not establish influence.
considerations: Possible influence without evidence it occurred maps differently from likely influence.

Likely influence requires more than assessor awareness or a possible pathway: look for evidence it occurred, or strong beliefs and a real judgement opportunity. Keep this conclusion separate from measurement susceptibility and detection opportunity.

questions.decision_rule: Distinguish possible influence without reason to believe it occurred from likely influence. Strong beliefs about benefits or harms make influence more likely, for example patient-reported symptoms or recovery assessed by an intervention provider. A standardized scale or grading rule does not by itself remove an elicitation, attribution, grading, or assessment pathway.

item.text: The protocol ties adverse-event collection to each participant’s treatment period, through 30 days after the last dose. Median treatment lasted 24 months in the abiraterone arm and 14 months in the placebo arm, so participants had different lengths of time in which grade 3 or 4 events could be detected. I’m recording this as a potential difference in ascertainment opportunity while treating CTCAE v4.0 itself as an appropriate grading method.

answers.justification: The article states that adverse events were graded using NCI CTCAE version 4.0, and the protocol describes coding adverse events with MedDRA and grading severity with CTCAE v4.0. This is a standardized method suited to the grade 3 or 4 toxicity outcome; no evidence indicates the method was invalid or insensitive.

The protocol defines treatment-emergent adverse events as collected from first dose through 30 days after last dose. The article reports median treatment durations of 24 months in the abiraterone group and 14 months in the placebo group, while safety was assessed at trial visits and treatment discontinuation. Thus the observation windows and opportunities to detect cumulative grade 3 or 4 adverse events differed between groups; the table reports proportions without adjusting for exposure duration.

This is a standardized method suited to the grade 3 or 4 toxicity outcome; no evidence indicates the method was invalid or insensitive.

The protocol defines treatment-emergent adverse events as collected from first dose through 30 days after last dose. The article reports median treatment durations of 24 months in the abiraterone group and 14 months in the placebo group, while safety was assessed at trial visits and treatment discontinuation. Thus the observation windows and opportunities to detect cumulative grade 3 or 4 adverse events differed between groups; the table reports proportions without adjusting for exposure duration.

questions.wording: Were the data that produced this result analysed in accordance with a pre-specified analysis plan that was finalized before unblinded outcome data were available for analysis?
questions.official_guidance: To avoid the possibility of selection of the reported result, finalization of the analysis intentions must precede availability of unblinded outcome data to the trial investigators. Changes to analysis plans that were made before unblinded outcome data were available, or that were clearly unrelated to the results, do not raise concerns about bias in selection of the reported result.
questions.source_locator: Full guidance p. 63, Box 11, signalling question 5.1
questions.bias_construct: Whether data producing this result followed a pre-specified plan finalized before unblinded outcome data were available.
questions.decision_rule: Compare the approved Result with the applicable plan for the exact intervention comparison, cohort, endpoint, time window, population, analysis, and effect measure. Distinguish source creation/version and amendment dates from trial events and retrieval time; only compare chronology when the relevant events and precision are established. Changes made before unblinded data were available, or clearly unrelated to results such as a broken machine, do not raise concerns.
evidence_needed: A sufficiently detailed protocol or SAP, its source-located chronology and finalization date relative to unblinded outcome data, and the reported analysis.

For an original plan and an amended plan, capture the source-located content and chronology separately. An embedded SAP can be applicable evidence when its comparison, cohort, and Result fields match; an absent or unresolved plan remains an information limit.
questions.no_information_rule: Use a definitive answer when firm evidence establishes timing and correspondence. Use a probable answer when source facts and trial circumstances support only an inference. Use no_information when neither is supported. A plan mention or matching endpoint alone does not establish timing.

answer_anchors.text: The result follows a sufficiently detailed plan finalized before unblinded outcome data were available.
The result did not follow such a pre-specified plan.
Analysis intentions or their timing are not sufficiently reported.

considerations: Assess correspondence between the applicable plan and the exact approved Result: outcome, time point, population, effect measure, and analysis must be compared.

Assess applicability before chronology: a platform or master plan may cover several comparisons and cohorts, so its presence does not establish applicability to the approved Result. Establish chronology separately: plan finalization must precede availability of unblinded outcome data; a source creation date, registry posting or update date, amendment date, or retrieval date is not automatically the relevant trial chronology.

Current registry content does not establish unseen historical intent, and a data cutoff is not investigator unblinding. Preserve unresolved applicability or chronology instead of filling the gap from report wording that merely looks prespecified.

Results-driven selection is a separate concern from whether a plan exists or whether its chronology is known. Do not infer selection merely from an amendment or from a mismatch without evidence that the choice was driven by results.

Neutral paired control: an applicable plan for the approved cohort differs from a platform plan for another phase; pre-unblinding finalization differs from ambiguous chronology only in the timing premise.
invalid_shortcuts: a protocol mention without date or detail
current registry content treated as historical intent
a data cutoff treated as investigator unblinding
a platform master plan treated as applicable to every comparison

n engl j med 377;4 nejm.org July 27, 2017
355
Abiraterone plus Prednisone in Prostate Cancer
Pain progression was defined as an increase of
at least 30% from baseline in the worst pain
category on the Brief Pain Inventory-Short Form
as observed at two consecutive evaluations per-
formed at least 4 weeks apart.
Assessments
Efficacy assessments included sequential radio-
graphic imaging to assess radiographic progres-
sion-free survival (CT or MRI and bone scan-
ning) performed every 4 months, starting at
week 16. PSA levels were measured at baseline,
monthly in the first year, and then every 2 months
until end-of-trial treatment. Patients underwent
serial monitoring of vital signs, serum hemato-
logic and chemical findings, liver-function tests,
and serum testosterone levels. Adverse events
were graded with the use of the Common Termi-
nology Criteria for Adverse Events of the Na-
tional Cancer Institute, version 4.0.
Statistical Analysis
The overall level of significance was 0.05, with
allocation between the two primary end points
of overall survival (0.049) and radiographic
progression-free survival (0.001) (Table S2 in
the Supplementary Appendix). For overall sur-
vival, 852 events were required at the final
analysis to detect a hazard ratio of 0.81 at a
two-tailed significance level of 0.049, with a
statistical power of 85%. An analysis of radio-
graphic progression-free survival was planned
when 565 progressions or deaths had been ob-
served, which would provide a statistical power
of 94% to detect a hazard ratio of 0.667 at a
two-tailed significance level of 0.001. Two in-
terim analyses were included (Table S2 in the
Supplementary Appendix). The overall survival
analyses incorporated the group sequential de-
sign with an alpha spending function that was
calculated as Wang-Tsiatis power boundaries
of shape parameter 0.2 (which shape the prob-
ability distribution). Secondary end points were
tested with the use of the Hochberg test proce-
dure to control the familywise type I error rate.
The primary statistical method of comparison
for time-to-event end points was the stratified
log-rank test, according to the stratification
factors. The Cox proportional-hazards model
was used to estimate the hazard ratio and its
associated 95% confidence interval.
Results
Patients and Treatments
A total of 1199 patients underwent randomiza-
tion from February 12, 2013, through December
11, 2014. Of these patients, 597 were assigned to
the abiraterone group and 602 to the placebo
group (Fig. S1 in the Supplementary Appendix).
The baseline demographic and disease charac-
teristics were well balanced between the two
groups (Table S3 in the Supplementary Appen-
dix). The results presented here are based on the
clinical cutoff date of October 31, 2016, for the
first interim analysis of overall survival, at which
time 406 deaths and 593 radiographic progres-
sions or deaths had occurred. At a median follow-
up of 30.4 months, the median time that the
patients received the intervention was 24 months
in the abiraterone group and 14 months in the
placebo group. As a result of the findings at the
time of the interim analysis, the independent data
and safety monitoring committee unanimously
recommended on January 12, 2017, that the trial
be unblinded to allow crossover among the pa-
tients in the placebo group to receive abiraterone.
End Points
Overall Survival
The first interim analysis was performed after
406 deaths (48% of the 852 deaths that were
included in the final analysis) and a median
follow-up of 30.4 months. Of these deaths, 169 of
597 (28%) occurred in the abiraterone group and
237 of 602 (39%) in the placebo group. The over-
all rate of survival at 3 years was 66% in the
abiraterone group and 49% in the placebo group
(Fig. 1A). The rate of death from any cause was
28% in the abiraterone group and 39% in the
placebo group (Table S4 in the Supplementary
Appendix). The relative risk of death was 38%
lower in the abiraterone group than in the pla-
cebo group (hazard ratio, 0.62; 95% confidence
interval [CI], 0.51 to 0.76; P<0.001). The treatment
effect of abiraterone on overall survival was consis-
tently favorable across nearly all prespecified sub-
groups (Fig. S2 in the Supplementary Appendix).
Radiographic Progression-free Survival
At the time of the analysis, the median progression-
free survival was 33.0 months in the abiraterone
group and 14.8 months in the placebo group

response_framework.firm_evidence_rule: The definitive versions (‘Yes’ and ‘No’) would typically imply that firm evidence is available in relation to the signalling question.
response_framework.probable_judgment_rule: The ‘Probably’ versions would typically imply that a judgement has been made. ‘Yes’ and ‘Probably yes’ have the same implications for risk of bias, as do ‘No’ and ‘Probably no’.
response_framework.no_information_rule: Use ‘No information’ only when both (i) insufficient details are reported to permit a response of ‘Probably yes’ or ‘Probably no’, and (ii) in the absence of these details it would be unreasonable to respond ‘Probably yes’ or ‘Probably no’ in the circumstances of the trial.
response_framework.independence_rule: Signalling questions should be answered independently: the answer to one question should not affect answers to other questions in the same or other domains other than through determining which subsequent questions are answered.
response_framework.quotation_rule: Brief direct quotations from the text of the study report should be used whenever possible to support the answer.

traps: A no-hit search describes one lexical query, not scientific absence.
A planned method does not prove conduct; a time origin or analysis population does not prove complete follow-up or equal assessment.
An endpoint label or definition does not prove objectivity, blinding, prespecification, or no alternative analyses.
A treatment assignment or visibly different intervention does not by itself prove that participants or personnel knew the assignment.
Different treatment or visit schedules do not by themselves prove that outcome measurement differed between groups.
Stratification does not prove allocation concealment.

questions.bias_construct: Whether the result was selected from multiple eligible outcome measurements within the outcome domain on the basis of results.
considerations: Use the review's prespecified outcome-domain eligibility criteria, not only the reported Result, and compare the reported measurement with all eligible alternatives. Keep the exact Result's comparison, cohort, endpoint, time window, population, and analysis scope fixed while doing so.

An applicable plan's correspondence and chronology are relevant context but do not themselves establish results-driven selection. The approved Result fixes the target being assessed; it does not erase other eligible measurements in the outcome domain or make their selection an observed fact.

If eligible alternatives remain unresolved, preserve no_information rather than treating the absence of documented selection as no/probably no. Eligibility is defined independently of which result was reported.

facts.text:
Treatment Allocation
Subjects will be randomly assigned to the active or control group in a 1:1 ratio after the
investigator has verified that all eligibility criteria have been met. Randomization will take place
across all study sites using a centralized Interactive Web Response System (IWRS). A country
by country randomization scheme will be performed using permuted block randomization.
Subjects will be stratified by presence of visceral disease and ECOG performance grade.
At randomization, the IWRS will assign a unique subject identification number to each subject.
The subject's identification number will be used on all study-related documents including
electronic case report forms (eCRFs). A treatment number will also be assigned to each subject.
This treatment number is the link between a subject's eCRF and blinded treatment group
assignment. Subject identification numbers will not be reused. Subjects withdrawn from the
study will not be replaced. All subjects must commence treatment within 72 hours (3 calendar
days) of randomization.
Blinding
The investigator will not be provided with randomization codes. The codes will be maintained
within the IWRS, which has the functionality to allow the investigator to break the blind for an
individual subject.
•
Under normal circumstances, the blind should not be broken until completion of the study or
the IDMC recommendation for unblinding is accepted by the sponsor.
•
The blind should be broken only if specific emergency treatment/course of action would be
dictated by knowing the treatment status of the subject. In such cases, the investigator may
in an emergency determine the identity of the treatment by contacting the IWRS. It is
recommended that the investigator contact the sponsor or its designee if possible to discuss
the particular situation before breaking the blind. Telephone contact with the sponsor or its
designee will be available 24 hours per day, 7 days per week. In the event the blind is
broken, the sponsor must be informed as soon as possible. The date, time, and reason for
unblinding must be documented by the IWRS, in the appropriate section of the eCRF, and in
the source document. The documentation received from the IWRS indicating the code break
must be retained with the subject's source documents in a secure manner. Subjects who have
had their treatment assignment unblinded should be discontinued from the Double-blind
Treatment Phase and entered in the Follow-up Phase.
•
Unblinding will be performed in the event that the IDMC recommends unblinding and
subjects are to be crossed-over to receive abiraterone acetate.

METHODS
In this double-blind, placebo-controlled, phase 3 trial, we randomly assigned 1199 pa-
tients to receive either androgen-deprivation therapy plus abiraterone acetate (1000 mg
daily, given once daily as four 250-mg tablets) plus prednisone (5 mg daily) (the
abiraterone group) or androgen-deprivation therapy plus dual placebos (the placebo
group). The two primary end points were overall survival and radiographic progression-
free survival.
RESULTS
After a median follow-up of 30.4 months at a planned interim analysis (after 406 pa-
tients had died), the median overall survival was significantly longer in the abiraterone
group than in the placebo group (not reached vs. 34.7 months) (hazard ratio for death,
0.62; 95% confidence interval [CI], 0.51 to 0.76; P<0.001). The median length of radio-
graphic progression-free survival was 33.0 months in the abiraterone group and 14.8
months in the placebo group (hazard ratio for disease progression or death, 0.47; 95%
CI, 0.39 to 0.55; P<0.001). Significantly better outcomes in all secondary end points
were observed in the abiraterone group, including the time until pain progression, next
subsequent therapy for prostate cancer, initiation of chemotherapy, and prostate-
specific antigen progression (P<0.001 for all comparisons), along with next symptom-
atic skeletal events (P = 0.009). These findings led to the unanimous recommendation
by the independent data and safety monitoring committee that the trial be unblinded
and crossover be allowed for patients in the placebo group to receive abiraterone. Rates
of grade 3 hypertension and hypokalemia were higher in the abiraterone group.
CONCLUSIONS
The addition of abiraterone acetate and prednisone to androgen-deprivation therapy
significantly increased overall survival and radiographic progression-free survival in
men with newly diagnosed, metastatic, castration-sensitive prostate cancer. (Funded
by Janssen Research and Development; LATITUDE ClinicalTrials.gov number,
NCT01715285.)

Treatment Allocation
Subjects will be randomly assigned to the active or control group in a 1:1 ratio after the
investigator has verified that all eligibility criteria have been met. Randomization will take place
across all study sites using a centralized Interactive Web Response System (IWRS). A country
by country randomization scheme will be performed using permuted block randomization.
Subjects will be stratified by presence of visceral disease and ECOG performance grade.
At randomization, the IWRS will assign a unique subject identification number to each subject.
The subject's identification number will be used on all study-related documents including
electronic case report forms (eCRFs). A treatment number will also be assigned to each subject.
This treatment number is the link between a subject's eCRF and blinded treatment group
assignment. Subject identification numbers will not be reused. Subjects withdrawn from the
study will not be replaced. All subjects must commence treatment within 72 hours (3 calendar
days) of randomization.
Blinding
The investigator will not be provided with randomization codes. The codes will be maintained
within the IWRS, which has the functionality to allow the investigator to break the blind for an
individual subject.
•
Under normal circumstances, the blind should not be broken until completion of the study or
the IDMC recommendation for unblinding is accepted by the sponsor.
•
The blind should be broken only if specific emergency treatment/course of action would be
dictated by knowing the treatment status of the subject. In such cases, the investigator may
in an emergency determine the identity of the treatment by contacting the IWRS. It is
recommended that the investigator contact the sponsor or its designee if possible to discuss
the particular situation before breaking the blind. Telephone contact with the sponsor or its
designee will be available 24 hours per day, 7 days per week. In the event the blind is
broken, the sponsor must be informed as soon as possible. The date, time, and reason for
unblinding must be documented by the IWRS, in the appropriate section of the eCRF, and in
the source document. The documentation received from the IWRS indicating the code break
must be retained with the subject's source documents in a secure manner. Subjects who have
had their treatment assignment unblinded should be discontinued from the Double-blind
Treatment Phase and entered in the Follow-up Phase.
•
Unblinding will be performed in the event that the IDMC recommends unblinding and
subjects are to be crossed-over to receive abiraterone acetate.
